questions.q: Who climbed up a tree to see Jesus, and what was his occupation?
questions.a: The person who climbed the tree was Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.

questions.q: What complaint did everyone make when Jesus went to Zacchaeus’ house?
questions.a: They said, “Jesus has gone in to be a guest with a sinful man.”

questions.q: What did Jesus say about Zacchaeus after Zacchaeus announced his gifts to the poor?
questions.a: He said, “Today salvation has come to this house.”

questions.q: What did the people expect would happen when Jesus reached Jerusalem?
questions.a: They thought that the kingdom of God would appear immediately.

questions.q: In Jesus’ parable, where was the nobleman going to travel?
questions.a: He was going to a far country to receive a kingdom, and then he would return.

questions.q: What did the nobleman do for the servant who had been faithful and had earned ten more minas?
questions.a: The nobleman gave him authority over ten cities.

questions.q: What did the nobleman do for the servant who had been faithful and had made five more minas?
questions.a: He gave them authority over five cities.

questions.q: What kind of man did the wicked servant think the nobleman was?
questions.a: He knew the nobleman was a demanding man.

questions.q: What did the nobleman do with the wicked servant?
questions.a: He took away the wicked servant’s mina.

questions.q: What did the nobleman do with those who did not want him to reign over them?
questions.a: The nobleman had them killed in front of him.

questions.q: What kind of animal did Jesus ride on as he went into Jerusalem?
questions.a: He rode on a donkey colt on which no one had ever sat.

questions.q: What did the crowd cry out as Jesus approached the Mount of Olives?
questions.a: They cried out, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!”

questions.q: What did Jesus say would happen if the people did not cry out rejoicing?
questions.a: He said that the stones would cry out.

questions.q: What did Jesus do as he drew near to the city?
What did Jesus then prophesy would happen to the people and the city?
questions.a: He said that enemies would smash the city to the ground and that not one stone would be left upon another.

questions.q: Who wanted to kill Jesus as he was teaching in the temple?
questions.a: The chief priests and the scribes and the leaders of the people wanted to kill Jesus.

questions.q: Why could they not kill him at this time?
questions.a: They could not kill him because the people were listening to him intently.

commentary.text: The parable of the nobleman and his servants.

Verses 1–10 Those who sincerely desire a sight of Christ, like Zaccheus, will break through opposition, and take pains to see him. Christ invited himself to Zaccheus' house. Wherever Christ comes he opens the heart, and inclines it to receive him. He that has a mind to know Christ, shall be known of him. Those whom Christ calls, must humble themselves, and come down. We may well receive him joyfully, who brings all good with him. Zaccheus gave proofs publicly that he was become a true convert. He does not look to be justified by his works, as the Pharisee; but by his good works he will, through the grace of God, show the sincerity of his faith and repentance. Zaccheus is declared to be a happy man, now he is turned from sin to God. Now that he is saved from his sins, from the guilt of them, from the power of them, all the benefits of salvation are his. Christ is come to his house, and where Christ comes he brings salvation with him. He came into this lost world to seek and to save it. His design was to save, when there was no salvation in any other. He seeks those that sought him not, and asked not for him.

This parable is like that of the talents, Mt 25. Those that are called to Christ, he furnishes with gifts needful for their business; and from those to whom he gives power, he expects service. The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal, 1Co 12:7. And as every one has received the gift, so let him minister the same, 1Pe 4:10. The account required, resembles that in the parable of the talents; and the punishment of the avowed enemies of Christ, as well as of false professors, is shown. The principal difference is, that the pound given to each seems to point out the gift of the gospel, which is the same to all who hear it; but the talents, distributed more or less, seem to mean that God gives different capacities and advantages to men, by which this one gift of the gospel may be differently improved.

Christ has dominion over all creatures, and may use them as he pleases. He has all men's hearts both under his eye and in his hand. Christ's triumphs, and his disciples' joyful praises, vex proud Pharisees, who are enemies to him and to his kingdom. But Christ, as he despises the contempt of the proud, so he accepts the praises of the humble. Pharisees would silence the praises of Christ, but they cannot; for as God can out of stones raise up children unto Abraham, and turn the stony heart to himself, so he can bring praise out of the mouths of children. And what will be the feelings of men when the Lord returns in glory to judge the world!

Who can behold the holy Jesus, looking forward to the miseries that awaited his murderers, weeping over the city where his precious blood was about to be shed, without seeing that the likeness of God in the believer, consists much in good-will and compassion? Surely those cannot be right who take up any doctrines of truth, so as to be hardened towards their fellow-sinners. But let every one remember, that though Jesus wept over Jerusalem, he executed awful vengeance upon it. Though he delights not in the death of a sinner, yet he will surely bring to pass his awful threatenings on those who neglect his salvation. The Son of God did not weep vain and causeless tears, nor for a light matter, nor for himself. He knows the value of souls, the weight of guilt, and how low it will press and sink mankind. May he then come and cleanse our hearts by his Spirit, from all that defiles. May sinners, on every side, become attentive to the words of truth and salvation.
